The Province of Manitoba has lived up to its end of that agreement. The federal Government has not. From the answers to the questions that I asked of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) on this last week in the House, it became very evident that this Government has not yet decided whether or not to live up to that agreement.
That agreement is important to the people of the Port of Churchill. It is important to the people who work in the communities along the CN line, whether they be in Gillam, Le Pas, or in communities in Saskatchewan. It is important to the farmers of Saskatchewan and Alberta who ship their grains through that port, and yet this Government is not living up to its word to abide by that agreement, an agreement that was signed between the federal Government and the Province of Manitoba.
As I said earlier, the province is doing its work. It is putting into place the hydro line to the Port of Churchill and the other work that it committed itself to do. The federal Government- and I realize that the agreement was signed by a previous Government-is not living up to that agreement.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in the House that his Government, this new Conservative Government, would live up to federal-provincial agreements already in place; that it would not "rig" those agreements. He said that the Government would live up to those agreements, and that is not happening with the Port of Churchill Agreement. The fact that that agreement is not being lived up to, the fact that the work is not being done, the fact that the Treasury Board submissions are sitting on the desk of the Minister of Transport and not moving from there all relate directly to this Bill. If in this Bill the Government is going to be establishing some type of user-pay plan, then I think we have to know what that is before we pass it.
We have an agreement setting out what the federal Government is supposed to be doing in the Port of Churchill, and it is not doing that. We now have a piece of legislation pursuant to which, if passed, the Government will be able to charge the users of that port and other ports for certain work that is done in connection with those ports. Is the Government going to charge the work that was promised and should have already taken place in the Port of Churchill against future users of that port? Is that something the Government is contemplating? We do not know that.
The Government is not acting on what it should be acting on. This Bill does not do that in the very important area of how this Government is going to recover the costs involved from the shippers and other consumers of Canada's ports and waterways. This Government does not even have the honesty to indicate that that particular clause is in the legislation. 1 received this press release, and other Members of the House must have received the same press release from the Minister of Transport and it does not even acknowledge that there is a clause in the Bill dealing with cost recovery or with the user-pay philosophy.
Why not come clean? I am sure that this press release was sent out to the users of Canada's ports; I am sure that this
press release was sent out to all Government agencies dealing with transportation and port authorities and I suspect it was sent out to shippers. Why didn't it tell the truth? And if it didn't tell the truth, how can we trust this Government to make regulations that will benefit those who will be using our ports in the future?

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to say a few words on this Bill. First 1 should say that 1 will not use the word "hypocrite". I will not call any hon. gentleman in this House a hypocrite. However, I remember that in 1974 and 1975 when a former Minister of Transport, as a matter of Government policy, brought in user-pay, 1 would say without using that unmparliamentary word that the Conservatives were just as vociferous as we were in opposing that. Of course, for the past year 1 have had to watch the spectacle of Conservatives making speeches that Liberals made a year and a half ago while Liberals are making speeches that Conservatives made a year and a half ago. Wihout using that unparliamentary word, 1 leave the matter for the consideration of all Hon. Members.
Transportation costs in a country with our kind of geography, climate and thin and widely scattered population should be a relatively neutral factor so that we do not discriminate against people because of where they happen to live or because of where they happen to manufacture, produce, ship or receive their goods. That is why in Canada, more so than in western European countries which are small and densely populated, it is required, because of our history, and no matter which Party is in power, that general tax revenues cover the costs of instrastructure like navigational aids, air traffic control, weather forecasting and the like. Those are public utilities and everyone has to use them both directly and indirectly.
I accept the word of the Parliamentary Secretary because I do not think even the Government is so stupid that it would try to get 100 per cent cost recovery. However, to think that there can be any significant increase in cost recovery under the user-pay principle in order to fight the deficit without harming the people and our competitiveness with the United States is to be dreaming in Technicolor. I do not know of any charges imposed by the U.S. Coast Guard, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers or the American weather services. They do not make any charges and the United States has a lot more people, money and things to move than Canada.
If it is logical to impose a nominal user-pay charge on navigational aids, weather forecasting, lighthouse services and the like, then 1 submit that it is equally logical to impose a nominal user-pay charge on traffic lights, stop signs and pedestrian crosswalks. If it is logical to have that sort of principle in place in legislation or as a matter of government policy, then it would be logical to have some competition in the market-place. There should be more than one outfit making weather forecasts and providing navigational aids. The users
October 18, 1985

could then pick and choose according to the rates that are being charged. We know that that would not work, so there is a fundamental fallacy in the principle of user pay. Whether we are dealing with a nominal charge or with maximizing cost recovery to as great an extent as possible, the principle is self-defeating.
If we begin to impose additional charges on a port like Vancouver which has enough trouble as it is what with competing with Bellingham, Portland and Seattle just a few miles to the South, we will send the shipping to the southern ports. If costs are increased, no matter how nominally, for ports like Halifax, Saint John and Montreal, the ports on the northeast coast of the United States will be only too happy to take the business away from Canadian ports. The ramifications of that principle do not apply only to marine traffic. They then flow through to rail transport from Atlantic Canada and Montreal to central Canada and the Mid-West United States. We will lose that to the United States as well. It seems to me that the Government needs to take another look at that clause of the Bill. In fact, siA months would be enough time for the Government to do that.
There is one thing about this particular legislation that we like. We are now creating legislation that deals with pollution control and the environment in Arctic Canada and this serves as an additional notice to the entire world and particularly the United States that those are our national waters and not an international passageway. It allows us to strengthen our case.
The provisions regarding certification and pollution regulation are generally good. No doubt, my colleagues from Thunder Bay and Skeena will have some amendments to move in committee that will strengthen those provisions. It is all very well to have those regulations enshrined in legislation, but if we do not have the capacity to enforce them, we become a laughing-stock in the international community. We do not have the capacity to enforce even the minimal regulations that now exist. We need more inspectors and we need more people stationed in the Arctic. I would suggest the use of an Armed Forces brigade that would be rotated every two or three months. We should give the members of our Armed Forces some experience in cold weather. After all, Canada is an Arctic country.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to enter into this debate. There is an interesting question with respect to whether or not the Coast Guard station in my constituency is the most southerly in Canada. I think it probably is. Partly for that reason I felt it important to add my voice to the concerns which have been raised by some of my colleagues with respect to the introduction of user-pay principles in the provision of Coast Guard services.
Coast Guard services with respect to my constituency are of special and particular concern because of their connection with the tourist industry. The tourist industry has been identified by local economic development groups as the area in which we see economic expansion and job growth in our community. In fact, we find a great many people who come across the inland waterways in the Essex County area to take advantage of tourist opportunities on the Canadian side, both in Lake St. Clair and in the Detroit River. I fear that if we institute a system of fees which could be applied to pleasure boats this could become a serious disincentive to those people who make the choice to take advantage of the tourist facilities on our side of the water system in which people have invested.
I raise a point which has been stressed by my colleague from Regina with respect to philosophically questioning the idea of user-pay. I think it is fair to say that in the country we have a history of transportation infrastructure which is in place and which was built by the community for the community. It is something which has contributed to the development of our country. At this stage in our history the putting into effect of an alien principle, a principle outside of our traditions, needs to be closely examined. We cannot examine the matter closely with respect to this Bill because the details of how the user-pay principle would be implemented are not spelled out.

that Bill C-224, an Act respecting the national hymn of Canada be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour to rise today to speak in favour of my own Private Member's Bill which is entitled the National Hymn Act.
Private Members' Hour is a process which to some of us is absolutely critical in terms of parliamentary legislative life since many of us come here and are not able to participate actively and constructively in many dimensions of that life. Private Members' Hour is ours. 1 genuinely appreciate the process. Personally, I am even more delighted that the Government has indicated it is prepared to see the subject matter of this Bill referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. Other Hon. Members will agree with me that that in itself is a major victory since for years and years we were not able to have our Private Member's Bills move on in the process. However, as the reform of Parliament moves forward we will come to play an increasingly more significant role in the legislative life of the nation. That will only be for the good of the nation, and I thank the Government for agreeing to the process.
In terms of the Bill I wish to commend Dr. Kenneth Hicken, a professor at the University of Lethbridge, whom I suppose is also somewhat frustrated by the process since it was in February of 1984 that he approached me with respect to a national hymn. It was not before the House until February of 1985 when it received first reading. Today, it is being dealt with in terms of second reading and reference to a standing committee. We who are involved in the legislative process realize that is not a long time, but for a private citizen it seems like forever. I am sure he will be pleased that this Bill is moving on.
I would also like to commend Dr. Gaston Renaud, another professor from the University of Lethbridge who translated the hymn into French. Thus, it is a beautiful bilingual national hymn.
As Hon. Members become more familiar with the hymn and once it is referred to committee, they may find it to be appropriate as a national hymn for Canada. I realize that in the committee other songs will be considered to fill the role of a national hymn for the country. While the hymn which is being considered now may not be selected as the national hymn for Canada, Dr. Hicken deserves an incredible amount of credit for commencing the process.
Some object to the idea of Canada having a national hymn. I disagree with that. In the public life of a nation it is these types of national symbols which can see a nation through bad
times as well as good. We have a national anthem which is for great patriotic events and July 1, celebrations where the country is happy. However, it is good to have a hymn to handle the crises in our nation. After all, we will face crises as we go on. Perhaps a national hymn would be appropriate for the death of leading Canadians and more appropriately sung than the national anthem. I believe it is a valid idea. I do not intend to speak any more because I wish to hear from other Members of the House in order that they can put their Parties' views forward.

It is a great honour for me to speak on the Bill which was introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), for whom 1 have nothing but the greatest respect. It is also appropriate to congratulate the Hon. Member for introducing this important Bill since it gave me the chance to explore the question of national symbols as I sought to inform myself for this discussion. I might mention that in my research I had the good fortune to come across the transcript of a broadcast interview carried out by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and, as it happens, it was with the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills.
I would like to say at the outset that I thought it was admirably candid of the Hon. Member to acknowledge the fact that the inspiration for the hymn came not from him but from one of his constituents, Dr. Kenneth Hicken, a professor at the University of Lethbridge. He composed the music and wrote the lyrics. It was translated into French by another University of Lethbridge professor, Dr. Gaston R. Renaud. His admission came in response to a question which I suspect is common to many Canadians, namely, why do we need a national hymn in this country? The Hon. Member replied in these words, and I quote:
Well, I think Dr. Hicken hit the nail on the head when this country's come through some real tough times ... and so he simply decided that what he needed, in view of the moral situation of the country, and the East-West antipathies, and the French-English problems ... that we needed to have a national hymn to remind us that there's more to living than just our own lives-
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, when Professor Hicken got to thinking about the need for a national hymn, he sat down and composed one.
In that CBC interview, the Hon. Member suggested that for very special, solemn occasions-particularly if the Queen were here-Canada could have what he called a triad of God Save the Queen, our national anthem, O Canada, and the national hymn. He suggested its use would be limited to times of national crisis when we are trying to bring people together. A national emergency, perhaps, or wartime, would be an appropriately important time to have a national hymn. He went on to say that while our national anthem is excellent, and the proposed hymn is in no way intended to supplant it, there are occasions where you would want something more solemn,
October 18, 1985

something along the lines of when the Americans employ their hymn America the Beautiful. It would, he said, be a kind of companion to the national anthem.
The Hon. Member said he is pleasantly surprised at the number of people who support the idea of a national hymn and indicated that while he is proud of the Hicken hymn, he feels that, if the Government and Parliament favour the principle of a national hymn, it might be well to open the matter to a country-wide submission of hymns. He foresaw a sort of hymn-writing competition, and it is here that I am strongly in agreement with the Hon. Member. I am one who is enormously stirred by the strains of O Canada sung sincerely, and I trust Canadians of whatever descent will never cease to respond with pride to our anthem.
A national anthem, like a national flag, is an important external symbol of nationhood. I had the pleasure, as a backbencher in a previous Parliament, of introducing a Private Members' Bill to have O Canada recognized as Canada's official national anthem. Of course, as a back-bencher in the Opposition that did not happen, but I had the honour of being the official spokesman for the Conservative Party. The Government of the day brought in legislation which finally brought the idea to fruition.
I feel, however, that the words to O Canada have not been publicized enough and a lot more should be done. I also feel the need for more songs celebating our land. It is at this point that I would venture to offer a refinement to my hon. colleague. Would he agree that a national competition to write songs about Canada would be a very beneficial exercise and that they need not have a religious connotation in the way of a national hymn?
We all recognize that about one third of our fellow Canadians are of a lineage other than native-French or Anglo-Celt-and that, consequently, a number of our fellow citizens follow religious beliefs which would not necessarily square with the sentiments of a conventional hymn.
As I mentioned earlier, I have taken the opportunity to look into the question of national symbols and how they have evolved. We have a wealth of symbols, all of which play an important role in our life. They represent and project a image of our country, they provide a link with our heritage and give us a feeling of continuity and serve to give each of us a concept of our identity. The history of the maple leaf as a Canadian emblem is almost as long as that of the beaver. It has been stated that the maple leaf was considered as an emblem as early as 1700. For years the maple leaf has been used as a symbol and identity mark for regimental badges of the Canadian forces. Since 1965 it has been part of our national flag. The beaver, which portrays diligence and hard work, was used as an emblem by the Huron Indians and first appeared as a heraldic symbol of Canada on a coat of arms granted in 1633.
Symbols have the capacity of expressing varied and often complex ideas through imagery. The symbolism of flags, emblems and coats of arms reflect the ideologies, history, beliefs and aspirations of a nation's people. I would argue, Mr. National Hymn Act
Speaker, that a nation's symbols must truly reflect the nation as it is, and as it is perceived by its people, or at least the overwhelming majority of them.
It would be a brave individual who would attempt to define a consensus on the matter of national symbols. Alas, he or she would have to wrestle with the perennial Canadian problem of identity. I came across an interesting letter recently in the Toronto Daily Star. The writer was dealing with the multicultural quality of our society and wrote that there are some 70 languages in use now in Ontario and that more than 50 per cent of Metro-Toronto's population is from outside the country. The letter dealt with the problem of Canadian identity and noted that Canadians often refer critically to the "overdeveloped America flag-waving brand of nationalism". He said, "This rah-rahing has served the U.S. very well, thank you. Maybe it is this fervency we are actually looking for". Which brings me, Mr. Speaker, back to my thesis. I wish to support the spirit of this Bill, but more, I wish to support the observation of its sponsor that we ought to encourage a national competition. My preference would be for a competition to write songs to glorify our country, to sing the praises of Canada and its regions and not specifically in the form of a hymn.
I am not sure whether the entire populace should be turned loose on this kind of contest or whether it should be an invitational competition among the known top song-writers of the country, people like Gordon Lightfoot, Bobby Gimby, and others. After all, we have produced a wealth of Canadian musical talent from Oscar Peterson and Joni Mitchell to Anne Murray and Hank Snow. As someone said, Mr. Speaker, we are not short of symbols which remind us that we live in a unique country and that we have a heritage which we treasure. We are, however, short of musical symbols, and the Hon. Member's Bill, while contemplating a national hymn, has much merit in requiring that we give thought to music to celebrate our nation. It is in this spirit, Mr. Speaker, that I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
Bill C-224, An Act respecting the national hymn of Canada,
be not now read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the Bill
withdrawn and the subject-matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee
on Communications and Culture.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL HYMN ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The motion, I believe, is a practical motion and I would not, of course, wish to oppose it. However, since this was scheduled for debate, I do wish to make some comments on both the substance of the motion as it has now been moved and on the only example which illustrates

October 18, 1985
National Hymn Act
the possible content of the motion which is before us. If this is going to be discussed in committee, I would hope that Members of the Committee would take into account certain matters which are illustrated in the hymn we have here, for example, the word "native" as in "our native land". Canada is my native land. It is my mother and father's native land and the native land of some others of my ancestors. However, it is not the native land of most of the people who live in my constituency in the usual sense of the word. There are also the aboriginal peoples of Canada for whom it has, perhaps-I do not really know-an ironic twist. They are not in a sense any more native than someone who is born here but they are aware of the historic division between themselves and us over this issue. So that I would hope that the committee would look-if it's going to choose a hymn-would look for one that steers clear of that kind of difficulty. There's another type of difficulty altogether in the word "thee" and the word "thou". "We raise our thanks to-God for thee". This is a usage which is beginning to disappear, at least in the English language. I don't wish to comment on the French usage, but to the extent that a song of this sort may be used in English, we have to consider the fact that the word "thee" has changed its meaning over the last four centuries in this sense; although it still is used to address a single person rather than a group which we address by "you", it is almost never used now except to address God. In the time of Queen Elizabeth I of England it was used very often to address any person. Since that time there was an attempt to continue that usage in English by people such as the Quakers who considered that to address a person as "thee" or "thou" was very properly intimate and that one should talk to members of one's family, to close friends and to God as "thee" or "thou" as grammar might indicate. However, the big majority, a very great majority of the users of English now use "you" to address even the closest members of the family. "Thee" or "thou" is very little used for intimacy or for the individual relationship.
So what happens then in the English language when we use "thee" or "thou" to address God we put him away off in the sky. We put him farther away than anybody else. Instead of the usage, for example, that we have in the King James Bible, which used Elizabethan English, and which also said in the psalm that God is closer then breathing, closer to me than my own breath, a very strong sense of intimacy with God notwithstanding his power. Now this word "thee" and the word "thou" put him off at the far end of the universe. That I regret. There are many people now who are changing the words of hymns and prayers in English so as no longer to push God away by addressing him as of "thee" or "thou".
Another change that is becoming much more common is to try to write our hymns in a way that does not exclude half the human race from being of the same sex as God, does not call God exclusively "him" or "he". I see some people smile at that but I don't find generally the women in my church smiling at that as though that were a silly idea. I find there is a strong feeling amongst many of the women and men in the Anglican
Church that we should find ways of addressing ourselves to God through word symbols that do not separate earthly men and women, do not make God exclusively male. I would hope that if we were to choose any hymn such as this for Canada we would bear that in mind.
I have one other concern with this particular hymn and that is that there seems to be really very little content to it except a kind of self-congratulation put into the language of the worship of God, that we're so glad that God has done such a good job of making Canada a good country and us good people and it's not clear whether he's the lucky one or we're the lucky ones.
This is a problem that has bedevilled-I use that word advisedly-has bedevilled worshippers certainly throughout the known history of the Jewish religion and the Christian religion and probably, for all I know, in the other religions of the world as well and amongst the people who conscientiously try to avoid any religious attachment. The form in which we find it in what Christians all the Old Testament is most clearly where the prophets preach against idolatry. Idolatry in their day was not a funny little superstitious use of images of stone or something like that. That was only the form of it. The idolatry of their day was a matter of the glorification of the state and the identifying of the state with the deity and that if you are against the state you are against God and that if you worship God in any way that's a little bit different from what the state provides then you should be killed.
Now, there were different opinions as there were switches of power during those centuries in the area we now call Palestine-different opinions about who was the state and who got to say what's the truth about God and just how people are going to worship him or her. And they had, as it happens, a long tradition of thousands of years behind them already as seeing God as both male and female. That became a very bitter fight in itself. So I think we have to be very careful about a plan to impose on the people of Canada, by some kind of statement of authority, a hymn which identifies God with the Canadian state because the Canadian state imposed the hymn.
It is said we need one because we only use O Canada for great occasions. In fact, I find O Canada used on many, many occasions and I still find God Save the Queen used on many occasions. I don't think we have been lacking in some way to express patriotism in a conventional religious mode. However, if a lack is felt, if we need still another hymn, I see no objection in principle to having it, but I'm very uneasy at the idea that we should try to have a kind of imposed or enforced unity among us by using a hymn as a peptalk.
When I was in high school and university we had pep rallies, we had freshmen initiation, we had the usual horseplay and so on and it could be endured then because we were just kids, or almost kids. But I would like to leave that behind me as an adult and not engage in sort of pep rallies and peptalks, not treat the worship of God as a way, as it were, of trying to hypnotize ourselves into believing that we all agree on everything, we have no divisions and no struggles among us. That,
October 18, 1985

for example, if that is the picture some people have that we have no divisions and no struggles, it might be untrue to our present scene, but it certainly would be untrue to the Jewish and Christian tradition from which I for one come. Therefore, I have learned over the years what 1 didn't think about so much in my youth, 1 learned to respect the concept of the separation of church and state. I have my Christian faith. In fact I'm a priest of the Anglican church, but I don't want to push my religion on anybody else, not even by saying, "Everybody stand up and sing this hymn because it's our national hymn".
The history of Israel, and for that matter the history of the Christian church, shows that Christians have had, from time to time, the gravest heart searchings about the state, about the territorial Government, about the human authority, and there are times when Christians have had to rebel against the state. We can all find them in past history. It gets a little touchier when we look into the modern century, but in past history it can't be disagreed with. So I would favour the idea of having this opened up in a committee discussion and I would hope that a variety of songs might be considered. I have one-I don't have the full text here, I only have the chorus. It's a poem-

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL HYMN ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-224, an Act respecting the National Hymn of Canada.
This Bill, and I quote:
-would provide Canadians with a national hymn in both official languages and could be used on occasions of a sacred or patriotic nature.
Mr. Speaker, I would like my views to be read into the record, so that the committee examining the amendment to this Bill will be able to consider my comments in future debates on this question.
Needless to say, I agree entirely with the reasons behind this Bill. To love one's country is a legitimate and noble sentiment that all the Members of this House who are dedicated to the
National Hymn Act
well-being of this country can understand and share. It would, in fact, be moving to see the members of a community give free rein to this feeling by singing together a solemn national hymn.
This hymn could forge one more link in our national unity. It is a fact that we need certain links to maintain our unity. But what theme could be the inspiration for this hymn? With what theme could each and everyone of us be expected to identify?
Unlike most countries, we cannot say that we have a homogeneous culture. With the exception of a small minority, the people living in Canada today were not born here or at least their parents were not born here. In fact, a very considerable part of the population of Canada was born under foreign skies.
As geographers keep telling us, the physical characteristics of this continent make it entirely appropriate for trade to flow in a north-south direction. It would have been entirely logical to see Canada absorbed by the States south of the border, which would have made it unnecessary to create artificial barriers to the natural flow of trade and transportation. But we knew what we wanted, and struggling against time and tide, we have progressed along our narrow strip of intermittently populated land, from one far-off ocean to another.
And how did we manage to do this? By the only means Canada had to populate its vast territory: immigration.
We can read the following in the foreword to a book published under the title: The Last Best IVest and written by Jean Bruce at the request of the Multiculturalism Branch of the Department of the Secretary of State. It is a history of how the Canadian West was colonized, illustrated with many photographs from that time.
"As the great tide of settlers surged into Canada in the years 1896-1914, to claim the free homesteads advertised by the government, immigration officers laboured to record a bewildering variety of nationalities, languages and occupations."
"Inevitably, the breakdown was somewhat arbitrary and rough. "Austrian" immigrants included Germans, Bohemians, Moravians, Slovaks, Ruthenians, Slovenes, Servians, Croats, Roumanians and Magyars. "Russians" were often actually Jews and Germans, sometimes Lithuanians and Poles. Occasionally, "German" meant only that the settler had sailed from Hamburg."
Incoming "Americans" came, in fact, from diverse backgrounds. Language was a major problem, and sometimes it was compounded by illiteracy. Harried immigration officers often wrote their own crude approximation of difficult names upon the entry forms, and many immigrants used that version in the years that followed, and passed it on to their descendants. The variety of newcomers was infinite.

October 18, 1985
National Hymn Act
The period from 1897 to 1914 marked a turning point in the history of Canadian immigration. During that short period of eighteen years, Canada received more immigrants than during its entire previous history. During that period, more than three million immigrants landed on our soil to find a home. About
1,250,000	were from the British Isles, 1,000,000 from the United States, 800,000 from Continental Europe and 20,000 from the Orient, including India.
Mr. Speaker, one may conclude from this picture that these immigrants who came from all parts of the world were for the most part white Caucasians. However, we were not all white or Protestant or Catholic. Canada has had a Chinese community, for instance, for over 125 years, and we can say that the members of that community have contributed to a very large and profitable extent to the development of some of our large cities, especially in economic terms. They have made distinguished careers in many disciplines including the arts, science and the liberal professions. In Canada they have managed to preserve their language and a large part of their cultural heritage. How many are Christians, agnostics or members of other denominations? I have not the faintest idea.
Arabs as well settled in Canada a long time ago. In fact the first Arabs landed here over a century ago, and many more have since come to Canada from various Arab countries, so much so that a number of Canadian cities are now home to industrious Arab communities. The Arab community easily blended in with the Canadian people and, as it has done for thousands of years, it made a generous contribution to the western world. In mathematics for instance, the famous Arabic numerals are still in use the world over. The wealth of Greek philosophy, the mainstay of contemporary western thinking, was set aside during the Dark ages and would probably be forgotten by now had Islamic theologians not made painstaking research in the major libraries of Moorish Spain. Even in Canada the Arab community has been able to preserve its ancestral culture. In that case, however, the main religion of this group is well known, as evidenced by the many mosques we can see here in Ottawa and elsewhere throughout Canada.
A relatively recent phenomenon attests to the generous conscience of Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I am referring to the poor unfortunate people who were chased right out of the bloodied lands of Southeast Asia, the Boat People as they came to be known. Those human beings of strong character had to live through experiences they did not deserve, but they were brought here in great numbers to live within our heartwarming and generous society where they were provided with the means to build a new and happy life for themselves. And they are proving to us that, humanitarian considerations aside, it was a sound investment for Canada.
In short, Canada is a genuine multicultural society-an amazing discovery for those who have never thought of our country in such terms. But the fact is that one third of Canadians are not of native, English or French ancestry. Their
number is growing, just as the multiplicity of their countries of origin is widening, just as their numerous contributions to the growth and well-being of our country are increasing.
This trend is ever more apparent in our urban centres, and it is a reality which has significant consequences for all of us. Strictly speaking, Canada's diversity cannot properly be defined as a mosaic. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, a mosaic brings to mind a static and unchanging image, whereas the make-up of the Canadian population does change from day to day. 1 would suggest it would be more accurate to say kaleidoscope, reflecting as it does ever varied, ever new and ever dynamic patterns, with all the challenges such a situation represents for us elected representatives of the people.
The Federal Government believes that the people are indeed Canada's finest resources. We believe also that our wealth is based not only on a wide variety of resource industries such as fisheries, forestries, mining, and vast agricultural lands such as those found in my great riding of Argenteuil-Papineau, but also on the diversity of our human resources, which are a major factor in the enrichment of our multicultural society.
The bottom line is that multiculturalism represents for every Canadian man and woman his or her country, people and culture.
To return to my question, what common theme could we use to conjure up a collective ideal? We have a number of symbols which are readily understandable and acceptable. The beaver is first and foremost in my mind. This industrious little animal, even though it is often a source of headaches for many landowners because of the dams which it builds and which flood farmlands and woodlots, is a perfect example of unremitting effort. The maple leaf, which is represented on our national flag, is also quite distinctive. It calls to mind our huge forests which were used to build our first settlements and, thanks to its simple and easily recognized design, makes for a great national symbol.
For quite a long time now these two symbols have been universally associated with Canada. They have no trait which would characterize this or that culture in particular. They are perfect and could be readily accepted by the Canadian people as a whole. Beside dedication to work which is a trait often associated with the beaver, they embody no idea or ideal which would require a careful scrutiny.
Such is not the case of the new hymn. I share the feelings which it expresses. But I do so simply because I am a Christian. But there certainly are a great many good and loyal Canadians who are not Christian. Their freedom of religion is guaranteed by our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Our National Anthem is part of our heritage and it has been more and more popular for over a century. And few people really
October 18, 1985

object to the verse "il sait porter la croix". But to impose outright a new hymn which has not stood the test of years to a great many people whose freedom of religion is guaranteed by the Constitution would certainly not contribute to the unity of the Canadian people.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL HYMN ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to participate in the debate on the motion presently before the House. 1 would like to begin by congratulating the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) for his initiative. I also congratulate Dr. Kenneth Hicken the composer and Dr. Renaud the translator of the hymn. This hymn as well as others should be considered by the committee when it looks into this important matter of national symbols and a national hymn. This subject has caused some difficulty in Canadian history, perhaps one with which we have not always been comfortable.
1 remember reading an article by a professor at Queen's University, I believe in 1958, who asked the rhetorical question, is that anyone in this country who noticed or is interested in the fact that although Canada is unquestionably an independent country we do not seem to have the usual national symbols characteristic of an independent country?
In 1958 we did not have an official national anthem. We did not have an official or a distinctive Canadian flag. That situation gradually changed. A consensus developed on both issues, the national flag and the anthem, less so in the former case. The flag debate was a very emotional debate in 1965 and I believe a very difficult one.
1 grew up in the 1960s. Only just a few years after the flag sitting at the right hand of you, Mr. Speaker, became our national flag everyone accepted it, yet it had been the centre of so much controversy and debate.
0	Canada is a fairly old tune in Canadian history. Its acceptance as our national anthem came gradually for many people. As a child in Niagara Falls in kindergarden in the late 1950s in the first song we were taught on the first day of school was God Save The Queen. I remember seeing a hockey game in Detroit. The U.S. and Canadian national anthems were played as part of tradition. I heard O Canada and 1 was curious. Why would they not be playing God Save The Queen? My father pointed out to me that O Canada was more distinctive of Canada and it was appropriate in international fora for
0	Canada to be played.
In the last four years of public school both O Canada and God Save The Queen were played every morning. By the time
1	got to high school in 1967 only O Canada was played.
1	have noted that the subject of O Canada being our national anthem has been in committee since 1968. I have a feeling, because of the controversy surrounding the debate on the national flag that parliamentarians lacked the impetus to get going on making O Canada official. By 1980, Parliament caught up with history, so to speak, and granted what was described as legal status to a heart-felt tradition. I believe the Bill went through with discussion but no dissent. There were certain problems that people perceived with the words of 0
National Hymn Act
Canada and, although it was proclaimed in 1980, Parliament had been looking at the question of O Canada and its words since 1967.
The committee issued its report in February, 1968 and unanimously recommended that the Government immediately adopt O Canada as our national anthem. In its recommendation, the committee slightly modified the original words as writtten by Judge Robert Stanley Weir, who I believe later became a chief justice of Canada. The original French was not changed. I feel that those who speak and understand French have an advantage when it comes to O Canada. As far as I know, there was no particular controversy with the French words. The controversy seemed to be about Robert Stanley Weir's words. Accordingly the committee, in its wisdom, adjusted slightly the words of O Canada at that time. As I said, when it was passed, there was no dissent.
When O Canada officially became our country's national anthem, the then Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton, the late Hon. Walter Baker, suggested that everyone in the House should stand and sing O Canada. I am sure it must have been a very moving moment in the history of this Chamber. The national anthem was proclaimed on July I and was sung for the first time in the Dominion Day ceremonies of 1980.
I mentioned earlier that the words were slightly altered. It was felt that in the original words there was a little too much repetition and that they leaned too heavily on the words "stand on guard for thee". 1 believe that line was in the song five times and with repetitions was repeated fifteen times. 1 think there was some justification for changing it. It was modified slightly.
At the time people really questioned all the words. They asked the question: For what are we standing on guard? Pundits were quick to point out the decline in Canada's military status, but I always felt that the words did not have a strict military meaning. I always felt that "stand on guard for thee" was just an expression of people's love for country. At the same time, when the military or the security of the country was called into question Canadians did stand on guard. In fact, going back to the War of 1812, and before, there have always been people who have fought for this land and were alsays there when Canada needed them. Therefore, as 1 said, because of the repetition there were some minor adjustments.
Other words were suggested, but those which were accepted changed "keep Canada glorious and free" to "God keep our land". I like that change. Certainly it was in accord with my own philosophy that I hoped God would protect the country which I loved. At the same time I appreciate the fact that there are those people who have a different conception of what God is and what God should be. When the committee looks at this, I hope it has sensitivity to the views of other people. I would be the first one to say that perhaps we will never reach a complete consensus on the words of O Canada. My guess is that when the committee looks at it and tries to decide on a national hymn, it will not be universally accepted.

October 18, 1985
National Hymn Act
It is the same with the national anthems of other countries. For example, if Americans sat down today to write a new national anthem I am sure it would not have the militaristic flavour of the present one. I think national anthems or hymns must be looked at in the context in which they were written. The Star-Spangled Banner was written during the British attack on Baltimore in the War of 1812, and of course reflects that.
This is one of the problems I have with continually making changes to the English version of O Canada. Surely the man who wrote the words considered O Canada to be a work of art. 1 have some difficulty with the idea that we should keep revising and updating them to current thinking. There is probably no committee of the House of Representatives of the United States cleaning up some of the language in The Star-Spangled Banner and getting rid of some of the militarism which is not quite in keeping with the standards of American society today.
The situation is the same with God Save The Queen. It was written at a particular time in British history. People have generally accepted its words.
When 1 talk about further changes to O Canada, most people indicate that they had enough trouble learning the old ones and ask us to leave it alone. 1 appreciate that there are people who have some difficulty with it. If 1 were to give any advice to the people who will sit down to review this question, it would be to ask them to look at the concept of a national hymn. I think it is a good idea.
These symbols of Canadian identity have been inspirations. They are something to which people feel very close. In the case of our flag, for instance, people feel a warmth about it. Someone mentioned a stirring when the words of O Canada are
sung, so I believe there is a place for a national hymn. However, there will never be unanimous agreement on a particular hymn or the idea that there should be a hymn. As far as possible the committee should be sensitive to the concerns of people when it actually makes a choice.
Before resuming my seat, I should like to conclude by congratulating my colleagues for their initiative in this regard.

Members will agree that if anyone else speaks, the motion will be killed and effectively the Bill will be killed. Therefore I ask of you, Mr. Speaker, to put the motion now in your fine style.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL HYMN ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL HYMN ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the amendment to the main motion?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL HYMN ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Agreed.
Amendment (Mr. Stewart) agreed to.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL HYMN ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion as amended?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL HYMN ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Agreed.
Motion, as amended, agreed to.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL HYMN ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Accordingly, the order is discharged, the Bill withdrawn and the subject matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
Order discharged and Bill withdrawn.
